Description
Identical Radio Management Panels
( RMP s):
Give the flight
crew control of all  VHF  radio communication systems (  HF
systems).
Provide backup
to the  FMGC s for controlling radio navigation systems ( ).
The two  RMP s are on the center pedestal (and the
RMP  3  is on the overhead panel).
Protections - High Angle of Attack Protection
High Angle-of-Attack Protection
In normal law, the aircraft is protected
against stall. This protection is also effective in dynamic maneuvers
or gusts. When the current  AOA  becomes greater than α PROT , the high  AOA  protection activates.  Without flight crew input, the  F/CTL  computers maintain the  AOA  equal to α PROT .
The  AOA  can be further increased by flight crew input,
up to a maximum value equal to α MAX . When the High  AOA  protection is activated, the normal law demand is modified
and the sidestick input is an  AOA  demand, instead of a
load factor demand.  The flight
crew must not deliberately fly the aircraft with a High  AOA , except for short periods of time, when maximum High Lift coefficient
is required (like during windshear or  GPWS  maneuvers).
AOA Protection
Vα  PROT , Vα Floor, Vα  MAX  are mainly computed based on the  AOA , and therefore
they vary with configuration, weight and load factor (
).  The  AOA
will not exceed α MAX , even if the flight crew gently pulls the sidestick all
the way back. The flight crew can hold full back sidestick, if it
is needed, and the aircraft stabilizes at an  AOA
close
to but less than the  1  stall. When flying at α MAX , the flight crew can make gentle turns, if necessary. If the flight
crew releases the sidestick, the  AOA
returns to α PROT  and stays there. As the aircraft enters protection at
the amber and black strip (α PROT ), the system inhibits
further nose-up trim beyond the point already reached. The nose-down
trim remains available.
At takeoff, the α PROT  is equal to the α MAX  for  5 .
This High  AOA  protection
has priority over all other protections.  The aircraft can also enter α PROT  at a high flight level, where it protects the aircraft from the
buffet boundary. Like in low speed or low flight level, if the sidestick
is simply released to neutral, the aircraft maintains the alpha for
α PROT . Therefore, when leaving a turn after entering α PROT , the aircraft may climb with the sidestick free.
Alpha for α PROT  is reduced as a function of Mach.
If the
flight crew flies into α PROT , they should leave it as soon
as other considerations allow. This is achieved by easing forward
on the sidestick to reduce alpha below the value of α PROT . The flight crew should also simultaneously add thrust (if the αFloor
has not yet been activated, or cancelled).
Between the α PROT  and α MAX , αFloor protection may automatically set the go-around
thrust. The αFloor will usually be triggered just after entering α PROT , and the go-around thrust will automatically be applied.
Therefore, if the sidestick is held aft, either inadvertently or deliberately,
the aircraft will start to climb at a relatively constant low airspeed.
To recover a normal flight condition, the α PROT  should
be exited by easing forward on the sidestick, as described above,
and the αFloor should be cancelled by using the instinctive disconnect
pushbutton on either thrust lever as soon as a safe speed is regained
(
).

ATC Mode
The selected  XPDR  is in  AUTO  mode.  In flight, mode S
continuously transmits information to other aircraft and replies to
requests from aircraft and ground stations.  On ground, modes A
and C are inhibited. Mode S (selective calling) and mode ADS-B (data
broadcast) are operative.
The selected  XPDR  is in  STBY  mode.  It does not transmit
either reply to ground stations nor to other aircraft.  The  TCAS  is also in  STBY  mode.
The selected  XPDR  is failed.
The link between  RMP 1 and  AMU  is failed. The
flight crew cannot change the  ATC  Mode.  If the flight crew
switches off the  RMP 1, then  RMP 2 and  RMP 3 display the ATC page with the last valid data know before the failure.  Or an internal failure
has occurred.
An internal failure has occurred.

How to Test the Mask
To prevent hearing
damage to the ground crew connected to the intercom system, inform
them that a loud noise may be heard in the headset when performing
the oxygen mask test.
Mask Stowage Box
On the  OXYGEN  panel:
CREW SUPPLY
CHECK ON
On the glareshield:
LOUDSPEAKERS  ON
On the  ACP :
INT reception
PRESS OUT - ADJUST
INT/RAD
INT
On the mask stowage box:
Press and hold
the RESET/TEST button in the direction of the arrow.
Check that the
blinker turns yellow for a short time, and then goes black.
Hold the RESET/TEST
button down, and press the  Emergency Pressure .
Check that the
blinker turns yellow and remains yellow, as long as the  Emergency
Pressure  is pressed.
Listen for oxygen
flow through the loudspeakers.
Check that the
RESET/TEST button returns to the up position and the  N/100%  is in the  100  position.
Press the  Emergency Pressure  again, and check that the blinker does not
turn yellow. This ensures that the mask is not supplied.
Check that the  Emergency Pressure  is NOT turned right in the direction of
the arrow (permanent overpressure). This ensures that the oxygen permanent
overpressure is not supplied.

turn yellow. This ensures that the mask is not supplied.

General
Operators may occasionally experience
high barometric settings above  1050  ( 31.00 ), due to polar anticyclonic air mass conditions. These conditions
mainly occur during winter in the upper northern region.  For departure and arrival, the flight crew must ensure that the aircraft
remains within its flight envelope.
When the  QNH  exceeds  1050  ( 31.00 ), the aircraft
pressure  altitude might be outside of its flight envelope (below  -1000
STD ), depending on the airfield elevation.  Operations at  QNH  above  1050  ( 31.00  ) are only
authorized within the flight envelope of the aircraft.
In addition, the flight crew should apply
the following procedures when the  QNH  is more than  1050  ( 31.00 ).
Refer to  FCOM  PRO-NOR-SOP
Standard Operating Procedures if no procedure is present in this section
(depending on the aircraft configuration).

Protections - High Speed Protection - Activation Condition
High Speed Protection
The aircraft automatically recovers,
following a high speed upset. Depending on the flight conditions (high
acceleration, low pitch attitude), high speed protection is activated
at/or above  VMO / MMO .
Protections - High Speed Protection - Pitch Trim Setting
When high speed protection is activated,
the pitch trim is frozen.
Protections - High Speed Protection - Pitch Trim Setting
When high speed protection is activated,
the  THS  setting is limited between the setting at the aircraft’s
entry into this protection and  11  nose-up.
Protections - High Speed Protection - Procedures
As the
speed increases above  VMO / MMO , the sidestick
nose-down authority is progressively reduced, and a permanent nose-up
order is applied to aid recovery to normal flight conditions.
Therefore, in a dive situation:
If there is
no sidestick input on the sidestick, the aircraft will slightly overshoot  VMO / MMO  and fly back towards the envelope
If the sidestick
is maintained full forward, the aircraft will significantly overshoot  VMO / MMO . At approximately  VMO  +  16  /  MMO  +  0.04 , the pitch nose-down
authority smoothly reduces to zero (which does not mean that the aircraft
stabilizes at that speed).
The  PF , therefore, has full
authority to perform a high speed/steep dive escape maneuver, when
required, via a reflex action on the sidestick.  The high speed protection is deactivated,
when the aircraft speed decreases below  VMO / MMO , where the usual normal control laws are recovered.  The autopilot disconnects at  VMO  +  15  and  MMO  + 0.04.
The  ECAM  displays an overspeed warning at  VMO  +  4  and  MMO  + 0.006.
At high altitude,
this may result in activation of the angle of attack protection.  Depending on the  ELAC  standard, the crew may have to push on the stick to get
out of this protection law.
Protections - High Speed Protection - Overspeed
In addition, if not armed nor activated
before the overspeed situation, the  A/THR  arms or activate
automatically and remains armed or activated while the overspeed conditions
are met. However, at anytime during the overspeed situation, the flight
crew may disconnect the  A/THR  if required (  and  ).
Thrust Lock Indication
Thrust Lock Indication
The  THR LK  message pulses after  A/THR  disconnection (action of the flight crew on  FCU  or failure)
resulting in thrust being locked. Both thrust levers being in  CL  detent or one in  FLX / MCT  (engine out)
detent.

How To Use
Set the baro reference of the standby altimeter to the appropriate
value.
Then:
To obtain the
correct altitude, add the correction to the altimeter indication
To fly at a
desired altitude, subtract the correction from the desired altitude.
Example
If the  QNH  of the day is  1072 , the baro setting on the standby altimeter should be  1049 . When reading an altitude on the standby altimeter, it is necessary
to add  600  to obtain the actual altitude of the aircraft.  Therefore, in this example, the indicated
altitude on the standby altimeter should be  1400 , in order to
fly at  2000
QNH .

General - Introduction
The slat and flap system includes
all of the following main components:
General - Slat Flap surface
Five slat surfaces
and two flap surfaces per wing. These surfaces are electrically controlled
and hydraulically operated. The flight crew extends the slats and
flaps by moving the flaps lever on the center pedestal. It has five
positions.
General - Slat Flap surface
Five slat surfaces
and two double-slotted flap surfaces per wing. These surfaces are
electrically controlled and hydraulically operated. The flight crew
extends the slats and flaps by moving the flaps lever on the center
pedestal. It has five positions.
General - Main components
Two  SFCC s, each containing one slat channel and one flap channel
A  PCU  which is made of two independent hydraulic motors coupled by a differential
gearbox. The motors use green and blue hydraulic power for the slats,
and yellow and green power for the flaps. The  POB  locks
the transmission when the slat or flap surfaces have reached the selected
position or if hydraulic power fails.
An  APPU  that measures the asymmetry between the left and right wings
A flap disconnect
detection system, which detects attachment failure and inhibits the
flap operation in order to prevent further damage. A sensor detects
the failure by measuring excessive differential movement between the
inner and the outer flaps.
The  WTB s which activate in the case of an uncommanded movement of the surfaces,
such as runaway, asymmetry or over speed. They cannot be released
in flight. They use blue and green hydraulic power for the slats and
for the right wing flaps, and blue and yellow hydraulic power for
the left wing flaps.
The  FPPU s that feedback position information to the  SFCC s
An  IPPU  that sends position data to the  ECAM .
If the flap  WTB  is on, the flight crew can still operate the slats, and
if the slat  WTB  is on, the flight crew can still operate
the flaps
If one  SFCC  is inoperative, both slats and flaps operate at half speed
If one hydraulic
system is inoperative, the corresponding surfaces (slats or flaps)
operate at half speed.

Climb - Initial Climb
Initial Climb
Normal vertical mode is  CLB  or  OP CLB  with managed speed active.
PF MCDU  PERF CLB
PF
MCDU  should be showing the PERF CLB page (allowing  PF  to monitor when the aircraft will reach the  FCU  selected altitude) but the flight crew may select other pages such
as F-PLN page as may be tactically necessary
The PROG page
displays OPT  FL  and REC MAX  FL . It is worth
noting that this OPT  FL  is a function of the  CI .
The displayed
REC MAX  FL  gives the aircraft at least a  0.3  buffet margin. The flight crew may enter a cruise flight
level above this level into the  MCDU  and the  FMGS  will accept it, provided that it does not exceed the level at which
the margin is reduced to  0.2 .
PM MCDU  F-PLN
PM
MCDU  should be showing the F-PLN page (allowing the flight crew to enter
any  ATC  long-term revisions to the lateral or vertical
flight plan).
Climb Speed Modifications
If  ATC , turbulence or operational considerations
lead to a speed change:
Select the new speed
with  FCU SPD  and pull.
Speed target is now “selected”.
To return to managed
speed mode, push  FCU SPD .
The speed target is now “managed”.
The best speed (and rate of
climb) for long-term situations lies between Green Dot speed and  ECON  speed. At high altitude, acceleration from Green Dot to  ECON  speed can take a long time.
Expedite Climb
If  ATC  requires a rapid climb through a particular
level:
Push the  EXPED  on the  FCU .
The target speed is now Green Dot speed.
Check  FMA :  THR CLB / EXP CLB / NAV .
Use the  Expedite
function  only for short-term tactical situations. For
the best overall economy fly at  ECON
IAS .
To return to  ECON
CLB  speed:
Push  ALT
Check  FMA :  THR CLB / CLB / NAV .

Climb - At the Transition Altitude
At the Transition Altitude
BAROMETRIC
REFERENCE  SET STD/CROSSCHECK
At the transition
altitude, the barometric setting flashes on the  PFD . The
flight crew should set  STD  on the  EFIS
CP  and on the standby altimeter.
Crosscheck the
barometric settings and the altitude indications.
Climb - Climb
Climb
CRZ FL  SET AS RQRD
If  ATC  clears the aircraft to its intended  CRZ
FL  or above, there is no need to modify the  CRZ
FL  entered in the INIT A page during cockpit preparation. The  MCDU  will automatically take into account a higher  CRZ
FL  selected with the  FCU ALT .
If  ATC  limits  CRZ
FL  to a lower level than the one
entered in the INIT A page (or present on the PROG page) the flight
crew must insert this lower  CRZ
FL  in the PROG
page.  Otherwise there is
no transition into  CRZ  phase: the managed speed targets
and Mach are not modified, and SOFT  ALT  mode is not available.
In that case, the  FMA  will display:  MACH / ALT / NAV  instead of  MACH / ALT CRZ / NAV .
Issue 2 :  The temporary
information is reissued to provide more information concerning barometric
pressure setting error, in accordance with EASA SIB 2016-05.
Issue 1 :  The temporary
revision is issued to advise operators that above the transition level,
when the flight crew selects  STD  on the  FCU ,
the last  QNH  or  QFE  barometric pressure setting
is transmitted to the ground, instead of the standard pressure value
( 1013 ).  Only the  FCU  selected
altitude, if used by the  ATC  on ground, may be misinterpreted.
The real aircraft altitude transmitted to the ground is not affected,
because the standard barometric altitude is transmitted, regardless
of the barometric setting selected on the  FCU .  In addition,
the  STD  value is correctly transmitted to other aircraft
systems.
Climb - At the Transition Altitude
At the Transition Altitude
BAROMETRIC
REFERENCE  SET STD/CROSSCHECK
At the transition
altitude, the barometric setting flashes on the  PFD . The
flight crew should set  STD  on the  EFIS
CP  and on the standby altimeter
Crosscheck the
barometric settings and the altitude indications.
When  STD  is set on
the  EFIS  control panel, the transponder does not transmit
to the  ATC , the standard barometric reference but the last  QNH  or  QFE  previously selected. The transmitted
aircraft altitude is not affected. Only the  FCU  selected
altitude, if used by the  ATC , may be misinterpreted.  Upon  ATC  notification of an incorrect barometric reference value, the flight
crew can manually select a barometric reference of  1013  and set again  STD  on the  EFIS  control panel.

GPS Interferences
Radio frequency interference can affect
the  GPS  data and the aircraft functions that use  GPS  data.
The aircraft can be exposed
to different types of interference:
GPS  Jamming: Type of radio frequency interference that degrades the  GPS  reception capability. The  GPS  data used by the
aircraft systems can be degraded or lost.
GPS  Spoofing: Type of radio frequency interference that makes the  GPS  signals erroneous, and that can result in erroneous  GPS  data used by the aircraft systems.
The following
table provides a list of cockpit effects that may occur during the  GPS  interference (the associated sequence of cockpit effects
cannot be predicted):

General
The Flight Guidance ( FG ) provides the following functions:
The Flight Director
( FD )
The Autopilot
( AP )
The Autothrust
( A/THR ).
The  FG  operates by
using the following modes:
AP / FD  lateral modes to control the lateral trajectory
AP / FD  vertical modes to control the vertical trajectory,
or the speed or Mach
A/THR  modes to control the speed or Mach, or the thrust.
Speed or Mach cannot be simultaneously
controlled by the  AP / FD  and the  A/THR .

When an  AP  engages, the sidesticks

pedals increases. However, the flight crew can always disengage the  AP s and the locking devices.  The  AP s engage with the same
guidance mode previously used by the  FD .  If the  FD s were not previously
engaged, the  AP  engages in

or  TRACK , and

aircraft pitch, bank angle, and speed are within an acceptable range.

Introduction
The  AP / FD  modes are either lateral, vertical, or common.
Two types of  AP / FD  modes are available in order to guide the aircraft:
Managed modes:
when the aircraft is using managed targets, the  FMGS  guides
the aircraft along lateral and vertical flight paths and speed profiles
computed by the  FM  from data in the  MCDU .  FM  manages the  guidance targets.
Selected modes:
when the flight crew is using selected targets, the  FMGS  guides the aircraft along lateral and vertical flight paths and
speed profiles to meet targets that the flight crew has selected manually
on the  FCU . The flight crew selects the guidance targets.

Loss of Cockpit to Ground Crew Communication on BAT Only
Description
When the aircraft is on ground and the
electrical power is supplied by the batteries only, the communication
between the cockpit and the ground crew is lost  1  after
the  BAT 1  and  BAT 2  are set to ON.
There is no maintenance message
and no  ECAM  alert when the communication between the cockpit
and the ground crew is lost.
The communication
between the cockpit and the ground crew is recovered when  EXT
PWR  is connected or  APU  is started.
Operational Recommendation
Alternate procedure must be established
and used by each operator for communication between the cockpit and
the ground crew.

General
The
RWY
mode is a managed lateral mode.  When the  LOC  signal
is available, the  RWY  mode gives lateral guidance orders
during takeoff, and initial climb.  The  RWY  guidance law aims to maintain the aircraft on the runway
centerline during the takeoff run.  When the
aircraft is airborne, the  RWY  guidance law aims to maintain
the sideslip indicator centered. To follow the guidance, the  FD  displays the conventional guidance bar.

An  ILS  (  GLS  )(  SLS  ) is set, associated to the takeoff runway, and the difference between
the  LS  course and the runway heading, as inserted in the
flight plan is less than  2 , and
No lateral mode is already engaged,
and

Autonomous Distress Tracking
The purpose of the  ADT  function
is to emit a signal in situations of distress or emergency, in order
to ensure that the  SAR  missions are accurate in time and
in location.
The  ADT  function autonomously detects situations of distress (e.g.
unusual aircraft attitude, loss of thrust, excessive cabin altitude
with no emergency descent, etc.) and triggers a distress signal without
any action from the flight crew. It also autonomously stops this signal
when the situation of distress ends.  This signal contains the following:
The identification
of the aircraft
The position
of the aircraft
The cause of
the distress situation
The time of
start of emission.
The  ADT  function
automatically triggers an emergency and a distress signal in the case
of impact, without any action from the flight crew.  The flight crew can also force the emission
of the emergency and distress signal by setting the  ELT  to ON ( ).
The  ADT  function includes
the following:
An  ELT  connected to the  DMC s
An  ELT  overhead panel ( )
An antenna on
top of the fuselage.

cases, which would normally lead to  ALTN  law, will degrade  F/CTL  laws down to DIRECT law, if the landing gear is extended.

GREEN DOT SPD (FINAL TAKEOFF,
GO-AROUND, DRIFT DOWN) : DO NOT USE
The Green Dot speed displayed
by the  PFD  does not take into account the extended position
of the  L/G . The flight crew should use the speed mentioned
in the TAKEOFF / GO-AROUND and EN-ROUTE sections below instead of
Green Dot when required.
TAKEOFF / GO-AROUND
After acceleration, and when flaps/slats are retracted:
SPEED  SELECT GDOT - 5KT
The flight crew should select
GDOT -  5  instead of Green Dot.
When GDOT -  5  is reached:
ALT KNOB  PULL
THR LEVER (REMAINING
ENG)  MCT
EN-ROUTE
DRIFT-DOWN SPEED : GDOT – 5KT
The flight crew should use GDOT
-  5  instead of Green Dot as drift-down speed.
EO MAX ALT  COMPUTE
The EO MAX ALT displayed by
the  FMS  does not take into account the extended position
of the  L/G . The flight crew should use an alternate source
to determine the  EO  maximum altitude.
FAILURE OF BOTH ENGINES
When both engines are failed, to ease
the handling of all the different  ECAM  procedures resulting
from this all engine flame out situation, it is recommended to use
the
ALL ENG FAIL
QRH  procedure, and if time permits, to clear
the  ECAM .  Follow all the steps of the  QRH  procedure, except those that are modified by the procedure below:
If  APU  is available:
Perform an assisted relight, when below  200 .
If  APU  is not available:
Attempt an  APU  start
If  APU  start is unsuccessful, a windmilling relight can be performed, as
long as the speed is above  260  (corresponding  N2  above  18 ). In this case, increase the aircraft speed and disregard  VMO  warning.
Flight controls are in direct laws. Use manual pitch trim as necessary
(not indicated on  PFD  if  APU
GEN  is
not available).

General
The
SRS
mode is a managed vertical mode,
used during takeoff and during go-around.  This chapter only describes the
SRS
mode during takeoff, also referred
to as the
SRS
TO  mode. The  FMA  announces the
SRS
TO  mode with the
SRS
indication.  The
SRS
TO controls the speed via the elevators,
in order to steer the aircraft along a vertical path.
The guidance law also includes:
A flight path
angle protection, that ensures a minimum vertical speed of  120
Engagement Conditions
SRS
TO  engages, when all
of the following conditions are applicable:
The aircraft
is on ground
The slats or
the flaps are extended
V2 is inserted
in the  PERF  TAKEOFF page  If V2 has not been inserted,  V/S  mode engages  5  after lift-off on the
current  V/S  value.
The flight crew sets at least
one thrust lever:
To the  TOGA  detent, or
To the  FLX - MCT  detent, when a  FLX
TO  temperature or a  Derated Takeoff  is
entered in the  PERF  TAKEOFF page.
When V2 is inserted, or
SRS
TO  is engaged, the speed automatically becomes managed. For more information
about engagement conditions of managed speed,  .

at the  ACCEL

*  or

General - Pitch
A pitch angle
protection to reduce the aircraft nose-up ( 18  of maximum pitch
attitude or  22.5  maximum in case of windshear).
General - Pitch
A pitch angle
protection to reduce the aircraft nose-up ( 15  of maximum pitch
attitude or  22.5  maximum in case of windshear).
General - Speed Protection
A speed protection
limiting the target speed to V2+ 15 .
General - Speed Target
When the aircraft is on ground,
V2 is the speed target.  When the aircraft is airborne,
V2+ 10  becomes the speed target.  If one engine fails, the speed target
is the current aircraft speed at the engine failure detection. However,
the speed target is limited by V2 and V2+ 15 .  For more information on the speed target,  .  For more information on the speed target,  .

From Soft Go-around to Thrust Reduction Altitude
The flight crew performs
a soft go-around when the thrust levers are set to TOGA then to FLX-MCT
detent:
The flight crew sets the thrust
levers to the TOGA detent:
A/THR  arms.
The engines
thrust increases to  TOGA .

SRS
GA  vertical mode engages on
the  FMA .
Then, the flight crew sets the

GA  vertical mode remains engaged.

A/THR  activates.

The soft go-around
function is only available with both engines operative. Therefore,
if one engine is inoperative, the flight crew must apply and keep  TOGA  during go-around. Then, to activate the climb phase, the
flight crew must set the thrust levers to the FLX-MCT detent.
If an engine
failure occurs when the soft go-around function is engaged:
The thrust on
the remaining engine is frozen at the initial computed thrust and
does not automatically increase to maintain the vertical speed target.
LVR TOGA  flashes on the  FMA  to remind
the flight crew to set the thrust levers to the TOGA detent.
General
If all  FD s disengage
while no  AP  is engaged, all the following occur:
The lateral
and vertical modes disengage, and
If engaged,
the  A/THR  reverts to (or remains in)  SPEED  or  MACH  mode.
If all  FD s disengage
while at least one  AP  is engaged, all the following occur:
The lateral
and vertical modes remain engaged, and
If engaged,
the  A/THR  remains engaged in the current mode.
Manual Disengagement
The flight crew can manually press the
onside  FD  to disengage the onside  FD .
Automatic Disengagement
The  FD  disengages if, in  ROLL OUT , the difference between the aircraft
track and the runway track is more than  20 .
Due to Failures
The  FD  disengages
if one of the following occurs:
The  FD  becomes inoperative, or
The  FCU  is not available, or
All the engines
fail.
Automatic Disengagement
Due to SPEED Protection
The  FD  disengages
if no  AP  is engaged and the aircraft speed is either:
below  VLS  in
DES
or
OP DES  , or
above  VMAX  in
CLB
or
OP CLB  .
After the  FD  disengages,
the  A/THR  reverts to  SPEED  or  MACH  mode and adjusts the thrust to recover the
target speed or keep the speed within the range from  VLS  to  VMAX , if the target speed is out of this range.
Disengagement Annunciation
If the flight crew disengages
one  FD , all the following occur:
The corresponding  FD  goes off,
The  FD  symbol no longer appears on the associated  PFD ,
1FD-  appears on the  FMA  if  FD 2 is disengaged or  -FD2  if  FD 1 is disengaged.
If one  FD  fails,
all the following occur:
All  FD  remain on,
Both  PFD s display the guidance orders from the remaining  FD ,
1FD1  appears on the  FMA  if  FD 2 fails, or  2FD2  if  FD 1 fails.

Pitch Bar

if one of the following occurs:
An automatic

General
The  A/THR  manages
the engine thrust.  The  A/THR  is either
armed, active, or disconnected.
When active, two different types
of  A/THR  modes are available:
The  SPEED / MACH  mode:
The  A/THR  continuously adjusts the thrust in order to maintain a Speed/Mach
target (e.g. during cruise, and approach).
The THRUST modes:
The  A/THR  controls a fixed thrust, in accordance with the engaged THRUST mode.
The  A/THR  modes are
automatically linked to the  AP / FD  vertical modes:
When an  AP / FD  vertical mode controls the trajectory (e.g.
altitude acquire modes, altitude hold modes,
V/S  /  FPA  ,
G/S  ,
F-G/S
),
the  A/THR  is in  SPEED / MACH  mode.
When an  AP / FD  vertical mode adjusts the aircraft pitch in
order to maintain a speed/Mach target (e.g. climb, descent), the  A/THR  is in THRUST mode.
When the
A/THR
is active,
the  A/THR  thrust target is sent to the  FADEC s. The  FADEC s computes thrust commands, in accordance
with the aircraft environment and status. The thrust commands are
then sent to the engines.  When the
A/THR
is armed, the  FADEC s compute the thrust commands in accordance with the thrust
lever positions, and the selection of  PERF  TAKEOFF page.  When the  A/THR  is disconnected, the  FADEC s
compute the thrust commands in accordance with the thrust lever positions.

Speed/Mach Target
The speed/Mach target is:
Selected  if the target comes from the  SPD /MACH value that the flight crew selects on the  FCU
Managed  if the target comes from the  FMS .
When in  SPEED  or  MACH  mode, the  A/THR  does not
allow speed excursions beyond the following limits, regardless of
the target speed or Mach number:
As a maximum
speed  VMAX  in high lift configuration,  VMAX  -  5  in clean configuration
As a minimum
speed:
For a selected
speed target,  VLS
For a managed
speed target, the maneuvering speed of the current slats/flaps configuration
( VAPP ,  F ,  S ,  GD ).
Speed/Mach Changeover
The changeover from  SPEED  to  MACH  or vice versa can be done automatically
by the  FMGC  or manually by the flight crew by pressing
the  SPD/MACH  on the  FCU .
A/THR Soft Mode
A/THR Approach Mode
Below  3200
RA , with at least  CONF  1, the  A/THR  behavior
is optimized:
Above  150
RA , to be more responsive to speed variations
Below  150
RA , to be less responsive to speed variations. This logic
exists to avoid large thrust increases during the lower segment of
the approach that may lead to destabilization and possible long flare.

General
The  FD  displays guidance
orders on the  PFD :
If no  AP  is engaged, the flight crew can manually fly the aircraft by following  FD  orders, or
If at least
one  AP  is engaged, the flight crew can use the  FD  to monitor the  FG .
There are two  FD s
referred to as  FD 1 and  FD 2. In normal operation:
PFD 1 displays  FD 1 guidance orders, computed by  FMGC 1
PFD 2 displays  FD 2 guidance orders, computed by  FMGC 2.

onside  FD  by pressing the onside  FD .

engage any  AP  or  FD , then
HDG
or  TRACK , and
V/S
or
FPA
engage. The  FD  symbol
flashes for  10 .

GA  mode, or

AP / FD
TCAS
mode engages upon
a RA.

landing capability

An  AP / FD  mode engagement
The approach
and landing capability (or the change of the approach and landing
capability)

First priority
is given to  F/CTL  messages
Then vertical  FMS  messages
Then  EFIS  reconfiguration messages.

LOC* Engagement Conditions
LOC
*  engages, when
LOC
is armed, and the aircraft reaches
the capture zone, or the pre-capture zone of the  LOC  beam.
Pre-Capture Zone of the  LOC  Beam (enhanced loc capture
function)
The pre-capture zone of the  LOC  beam is introduced through the Enhanced  LOC  Capture function.
With the enhanced  LOC  Capture function, the aircraft uses
the aircraft position and the  FMS  trajectory to provide
guidance in order to pre-capture the  LOC  beam.
The pre-capture of the  LOC  beam allows to:
Enhance the
performance of the  LOC  capture
Avoid a false
capture
Capture the  LOC  beam without overshoot.
The pre-capture zone is available,
when all of the following conditions are applicable:
The  LOC  deviation is more than 2.3 dots, and
The  FMS  is in
GPS  PRIMARY , and
The difference between the track
and the  LOC  course is between  25  and  115 , and
The roll order is such that
LOC
*  will capture the  LOC  beam with a single turn.
On the  PFD  and on
the  ND , the flight crew observes movement of the  LOC  deviation toward the center of the scale, only when the  LOC  deviation is less than 2 dots. This occurs when the aircraft is
in the capture zone.
LOC* Engagement Conditions - Capture Zone of the LOC Beam
Capture Zone of the LOC Beam
The aircraft reaches the capture
zone of the  LOC  beam, when one of the following occurs:
The  LOC  deviation is less than 2.3 dots, and:
The difference
between the track and the  LOC  course is between  25  and  115  , and
The roll order
is such that
LOC
*  will capture the  LOC  beam with a single turn.
The  LOC  deviation is less than 1.3 dot, and the difference between the track
and the  LOC  course is less than  15 .
If the approach is an  ILS , the
LOC
*  mode uses the  ILS
LOC  deviation to perform the capture.
During the  LOC  capture, the  LOC  deviation starts to move toward the
center of the LS scale, on the  PFD  and  ND , when
the  LOC  deviation is less than 2 dots.
LOC* Engagement Conditions - LOC Convergence Function
LOC Convergence Function
The purpose of the  LOC  convergence function is to help to intercept and capture the  LOC  axis.
The flight guidance intercepts
the  LOC  axis with a  20  track convergence,
when all the following conditions are applicable:
The
LOC
mode is armed, and
The
NAV
mode is engaged, and
The aircraft
is within  20  of the destination runway, and
The difference
between the aircraft track and the runway course is less than  20 .

General
The
LAND
mode is a common vertical and lateral mode.  The
LAND
mode tracks
the  LOC  and  G/S  beams from  400
RA  to approximately  40
RA .
Engagement Conditions
LAND
automatically engages, when all
the following conditions are applicable:
The approach
and landing capability is  CAT1 ,  CAT2  or  CAT3 , and
LOC
and
G/S
are engaged, and
The aircraft
is below  400
RA .
Disengagement Conditions
LAND  automatically disengages:
When the aircraft
approximately reaches  40  RA:  FLARE  engages, or
When the flight
crew disengages both  AP / FD , or
When the flight
crew performs a go-around.
General
The  FLARE  mode is a common lateral and vertical
mode:
Lateral guidance:
The  FLARE  mode reduces
the sideslip angle, such that the aircraft will be aligned with the
runway centerline at the aircraft touchdown
Vertical guidance:
The  FLARE  mode decreases
the descent rate, in order to ensure a comfortable transition between
the glide tracking, and the aircraft touchdown
If the  A/THR  is active, the thrust is automatically reduced to IDLE.
Engagement Conditions
FLARE  engages, if all the following conditions
are applicable:
The aircraft
approximately reaches  40  RA
The approach
that the flight crew selects is either an  ILS  approach,
a
GLS
approach, or an  RNAV ( GNSS ) approach with  LPV  minima (with
SLS  ).
FLARE  engages only if the following conditions
are applicable:
The slats/flaps
are extended, or the landing gears are extended
One valid  RA .
Disengagement Conditions
FLARE  automatically disengages:
When
the aircraft touches down:  ROLL OUT  engages, or
When
the flight crew disengages both  AP / FD , or
When the flight
crew perform a go-around.
General
The  ROLL OUT  mode is a common lateral and vertical
mode:
Lateral guidance:
The  ROLL OUT  mode guides
the aircraft along the runway centerline
Vertical guidance:
The  ROLL OUT  mode lands
the nose landing gear.
Engagement Conditions
The  FLARE  mode
changes to the  ROLL OUT  mode when the aircraft
touches down.
Disengagement Conditions
ROLL OUT  disengages, when one of the following
occurs:
The aircraft
exits the runway, or
When the difference between
the aircraft track and the runway track is more than 20°, the  ROLL OUT  disengages due to the  AP s and  FD s disengagement.
The flight crew engages a go-around.

The
F-LOC
*  mode captures the  F-LOC  beam.  The

Final Descent Point
Definition of the Final Descent Point (also called Vertical
Intersection Point " VIP " for  RNAV  ( RNP ) approaches)
The  FDP  is the waypoint from
which starts the  FMS  segment with coded  FPA .
For  RNAV ( RNP ) approaches, this point may be
indicated on the chart as  FDP  or " VIP ".
This point is defined in the
Navigation Database by:
A constant vertical
flight path beyond this point,
A coded altitude
constraint that may be "at" or "at or above" (e.g.
+ 3000 ). This constraint is displayed on  ND  (in
magenta), next to the corresponding waypoint, when the  CSTR  key is selected on the  EFIS  Control Panel. It is also
shown on the  F-PLN  page at this  WPT .
The  FAF  is the position
from where the obstacle clearance is defined relative to an  OCS . Obstacle clearance is only ensured if the aircraft is flying on
the defined vertical flight path. Before the  FAF , minimum
altitudes are published with fixed  MOC . The  FDP  is the point in the procedure at or before the  FAF  from
which a constant vertical flight path is defined.

General
CLB  mode is a managed vertical
mode.
CLB
guides the aircraft vertically
along the  FMS  flight plan, to the  FCU  selected
altitude or to the next altitude constraint, whichever comes first.
Therefore, altitude constraints, associated with applicable waypoints,
are taken into account.
CLB
can only be engaged, when
NAV
is engaged.
When
CLB
is engaged:
AP / FD s controls the speed/Mach target (selected or managed)
through the elevators
The  FG  system does
not adjust the speed/Mach target to match the altitude constraints.
If the
A/THR
is active, the  A/THR  will control the thrust.
CLB
usually arms before it engages.
Arming Conditions
CLB
arms, when all of the following
conditions are applicable:
The aircraft
is on ground, or
SRS
TO  or
SRS
GA  is engaged, and
NAV  is armed or engaged, or the vertical flight plan is available, and
The altitude set on the  FCU  is above the current altitude, and
The  ACCEL  altitude
is available, and is below:
the  FCU  selected altitude, and
the next altitude
constraint.
CLB
also arms, when
CLB
was previously engaged,
and
ALT
CST
*  engages. This scenario
is possible, when the selected altitude set on the  FCU  is
above the altitude constraint.  The flight crew can display and modify
the  ACCEL  altitude on the  PERF  TAKEOFF and  PERF  GO AROUND pages.

disarms, when one of the following
occurs:

mode engages, or

The  FMS  flight phase changes to  DES  or  APPR  phase.

General
Go-around combines
SRS
GA  vertical mode, and
GA
TRK
lateral mode.
SRS
GA  and
GA
TRK
engage at the same time. They disengage
at different moment.
At go-around engagement (i.e.
SRS
GA  and
GA
TRK
engage):
The  FMS  flight phase becomes go-around
If not previously
engaged, the  FD s automatically engage
If  FPD / FPV  was previously displayed, it reverts to  FD  bars.
General
When the flight crew initiates
a go-around, the
SRS
GA  vertical mode engages. In addition, one of the
following occurs:
If a lateral
managed mode is engaged (except
NAV
mode),
GA
TRK
engages, and
NAV
mode arms
NAV
automatically engages as soon as
the aircraft reaches the capture zone of the flight plan active leg.
If a  HDG / TRK  was preset,
NAV
mode does not arm.
GA
TRK
engages, until the flight crew
pulls the  HDG/TRK  to follow the preset target.
Example: Go-around during an  ILS  approach
If
NAV
mode is engaged, it
remains engaged
Example: Go-around during an approach in  NAV / FPA
If
HDG  / TRACK  mode is engaged, it remains engaged,
and
NAV
mode arms
NAV
automatically engages as soon as
the aircraft reaches the capture zone of the flight plan active leg.
Example: Go-around during an approach in  HDG  /  V/S
Example: Go-around during an approach in  TRK / FPA
In addition, at go-around engagement:
The  FMS  flight phase becomes go-around
If not previously
engaged, the  FD s automatically engage
If  FPD / FPV  was previously displayed, it reverts to  FD  bars.
General
The  SRS  mode is a managed
vertical mode. This mode is applicable during takeoff and go-around.
This chapter is only about the  SRS  mode during go-around,
also referred to as
SRS
GA  mode.  The  FMA  displays
SRS  , when the
SRS
GA  mode engages.  The
SRS
GA  controls the speed
target via the elevators.
The guidance law also includes:
A flight path
angle protection, that ensures a positive climb
A pitch angle
protection to reduce the aircraft nose-up ( 18  of maximum pitch
altitude or  22.5 maximum in case of windshear)
A speed protection,
that ensures the aircraft does not exceed  VFE .
The speed
target is the memorized aircraft speed at
SRS
GA  engagement or  VAPP , whichever is higher.
The higher limit of the target
is the lowest value between:
25  above  VLS  (or  15  above  VLS  when one engine
is inoperative)
5  below  VMAX .
At
SRS
GA  engagement, the speed
becomes managed.
General
The  SRS  mode is a managed
vertical mode. This mode is applicable during takeoff and go-around.
This chapter is only about the  SRS  mode during go-around,
also referred to as
SRS
GA  mode.  The  FMA  displays
SRS  , when the
SRS
GA  mode engages.  The
SRS
GA  controls the speed
target via the elevators.
The guidance law also includes:
A flight path
angle protection, that ensures a positive climb
A pitch angle
protection to reduce the aircraft nose-up ( 15  of maximum pitch
altitude or  22.5 maximum in case of windshear)
A speed protection,
that ensures the aircraft does not exceed  VFE .
The speed
target is the memorized aircraft speed at
SRS
GA  engagement or  VAPP , whichever is higher.
The higher limit of the target
is the lowest value between:
25  above  VLS  (or  15  above  VLS  when one engine
is inoperative)
5  below  VMAX .
At
SRS
GA  engagement, the speed
becomes managed.
Engagement Conditions
SRS
GA  engages when all
of the following conditions are applicable:
The flight crew
sets at least one thrust lever to the  TOGA  detent
The flaps lever
is at least in position 1
The aircraft
is airborne, or on ground for less than  30 .
SRS
GA  mode
can be engaged regardless of the vertical mode (except
SRS
TO ).
Disengagement Conditions
The
SRS
GA  mode disengages when
one of the following occur:
At the go-around
acceleration altitude ( GA
ACC
ALT ), or if
ALT
*  or
ALT
CST
*  engages (above  400
RA )
If the flight
crew engages another vertical mode
If the selected
target altitude is above the aircraft altitude and the flight crew
selects a speed:
SRS
GA  reverts to
OP
CLB
If the
AP / FD
TCAS
mode engages upon
a  RA .
In Engine Out
conditions, the  SRS
GA  mode does not automatically
disengage at  EO
ACC
ALT .
In dual  AP  configuration, disengagement of the go-around mode, on either
axis, causes  AP  2 to disconnect.
Reversions -Triple Click
Reversions
When
SRS
GA  reverts to
OP
CLB  , the following occurs:
The triple click
sounds
The new guidance
mode is boxed for  10 .
General
The
GA
TRK
mode is a managed lateral mode
that is applicable during go-around.  The
GA
TRK
mode maintains the track of the
aircraft, when the mode engages.
Engagement Conditions
GA
TRK
engages, when all of the following
conditions are applicable:
The flight crew
sets at least one thrust lever to the  TOGA  detent
The slats or
the flaps are extended
The aircraft
is airborne, or on ground for less than  30 .
GA
TRK
simultaneously engages with
SRS
GA .
Engagement Conditions
GA
TRK
engages when all of the following
conditions are applicable:
The flight crew
sets at least one thrust lever to the  TOGA  detent
The slats or
the flaps are extended
The aircraft
is airborne, or on ground for less than  30
NAV  ,
HDG  , or  TRACK  is not engaged.
GA
TRK
simultaneously engages with
SRS
GA .
Disengagement Conditions
GA
TRK
disengages when another lateral
mode engages.
GA
TRK
cannot be disengaged below  100
RA .
Speed Target
When the
SRS
GA  mode disengages,
the speed target becomes the smaller of Green Dot Speed or the speed
constraints.
If the FMS flight phase is cruise,
the SPD LIM or the SPD CSTR are still respected.
Arming Conditions
When the aircraft
is in an overspeed situation above  400
RA :
The speed is
above  VMAX  +  5  in clean configuration, or
The speed is
above  VMAX  +  9 , when slats or flaps are extended.
A triple click sounds when the  A/THR  arms.
Arming Conditions
In addition,
A/THR
can be armed by a flight crew
action on the thrust levers, when the
A/THR
is active.
A/THR Disconnection
When the airspeed
reaches  VLS  after an  A.FLOOR  activation, the  A/THR  disconnects
if not connected before the  A.FLOOR  activation.
A/THR Disconnection
When the airspeed
reaches  VMAX  after an automatic arming or activation due
to an overspeed situation, the  A/THR  disconnects if not
armed nor active before the overspeed situation.
A/THR Disconnection
For more
information on how to the set the autothrust to off,  .
If the flight crew
presses, and holds one  A/THR
instinctive disconnect  for more than  15 , the  A/THR  will disconnect for the remainder of the flight. All  A/THR  modes, including
A.FLOOR  , will be lost. The  A/THR  will be recovered at the
next  FMGC  power-up on the ground.

Ground Speed Mini Function
General
When the aircraft flies an approach in
managed speed, the managed speed target, displayed by the magenta
triangle on the  PFD s, is variable. This managed speed target
is the  VAPP , displayed on the  PERF
APPR  page, corrected by the Ground Speed Mini function.
Activation conditions
The Ground Speed Mini function
is active when:
The speed is
managed
The  FMS  flight phase is the approach phase.
The Ground Speed Mini function
does not correct Green Dot, S and F speeds.
Principle
The Ground Speed Mini function takes
advantage of the aircraft inertia when the wind varies during the
approach in order to provide an appropriate indicated target speed
(i.e. the managed target speed represented by the magenta triangle
on the  PFD ). When the flight crew flies this indicated
target speed, the energy of the aircraft is maintained above a minimum
level that ensures standard aerodynamic margins versus the stall.  The minimum energy level is the energy
level the aircraft will have at touchdown with an indicated airspeed
equal to  VAPP , and with the wind equal to the tower reported
wind as inserted in the  PERF
APPR  page. The
ground speed then equals the Ground Speed Mini.  The Ground
Speed Mini is not displayed to the flight crew.  During
the approach, the  FMGS  continuously computes the managed
target speed in order to keep the ground speed at or above the Ground
Speed Mini.
Managed Speed Target Computation
Managed Speed Target Computation
The computation of the managed speed
target uses the tower headwind component, the current headwind component,
and the  VAPP .
Tower Headwind Component
The tower wind is the average
wind provided by the  ATIS  or the tower. The flight crew
enters the tower wind in the  MAG  WIND field in the  PERF
APPR  page.  The tower headwind component is the projection of the MAG WIND on
the runway axis. This computation is based on the runway inserted
in the  FMS  active  F-PLN .
Current Headwind Component
The projection of the current wind measured
by the  ADIRS  on the aircraft longitudinal axis is the current
headwind component (instantaneous headwind).
Managed Speed Target Computation - VAPP Computation
VAPP Computation
The  FMS  computes
the  VAPP , and displays it on the  PERF
APPR  page. The  VAPP  computation takes into account the tower
headwind component.  VAPP  is the highest of the following
computations:
VAPP  =  VLS  + 1/3 x TWR HEADWIND COMPONENT, or
VAPP  =  VLS  +  5 .
“1/3 of the TWR HEADWIND COMPONENT”
has 2 limits:
0  as the minimum value (no wind or tailwind)
+ 15  as the maximum value.
The flight crew can manually
modify the  VAPP  and the  MAG  WIND values on the  PERF
APPR  page.
Managed Speed Target Computation
Managed Speed Target Computation
The  FG  continuously computes
the managed speed target that is equal to  VAPP  plus an
additional increment. This increment takes into account the headwind
variation during the final approach.  Managed speed target =  VAPP  + (CURRENT HEADWIND COMPONENT - TWR HEADWIND COMPONENT).  The managed speed target has the following
limits:
VAPP , as the minimum value
VFE  next, in  CONF  0, 1, 2, 3,  VFE  -  5  in  CONF  FULL, as the maximum value.
Managed Speed Target Computation
Managed Speed Target Computation
The  FG  continuously computes
the managed speed target that is equal to  VAPP  plus an
additional increment. This increment takes into account the headwind
variation during the final approach.  Managed speed target =  VAPP  + 1/3 x (CURRENT HEADWIND COMPONENT - TWR HEADWIND COMPONENT).  The managed speed target has the following
limits:
VAPP , as the minimum value
VFE  next, in  CONF  0, 1, 2, 3,  VFE  -  5  in  CONF  FULL, as the maximum value.
Disengagement Conditions
Managed speed disengages any
time the flight crew selects a speed target on the  FCU ,
or if the speed was preselected.
General
When the speed target is selected, the  SPD /MACH window of the  FCU  displays this speed target.  The  PFD  displays the associated speed target on the airspeed
scale. The flight crew uses the knob on the  FCU  to set
this speed target.  For more information on the Speed/Mach
Control Area,  .  For more information on the PFD Airspeed
Indications,  .
If the selected speed/Mach target
is set below VLS or above VMAX, with the autothrust active, the  FMGS  automatically limits the speed to:
VLS , or
VMAX  in the case  VMAX  is equal to  VFE , or
VMAX  -  5  in the case  VMAX  is equal to  VMO / MMO .
Selected speed has priority
over managed speed. The only automatic change-over from selected to
managed speed target may occur at go-around mode engagement.  In flight,
if the situation calls for managed speed, both the  PFD  and
the  MCDU  display a message proposing a manual change to
managed speed (for example  SET MANAGED SPEED ,  CHECK SPEED MODE ,  SET HOLD SPEED ).

Speed/MACH Switching
Speed/Mach switching can be
automatic, or manual.  The speed/Mach target (selected
or managed) is displayed on the  FCU .  The flight crew may check the speed/Mach
target computed by the  FMS  at the crossover altitude in
the PERF page.
Automatic Switching
During climb, at the crossover
altitude, the speed target (selected or managed) automatically changes
to the associated Mach target.  During descent, at the crossover
altitude, the Mach target (selected or managed) automatically changes
to the associated speed target.
The flight crew may enter a
speed target in the PERF CLB page, or a speed/Mach target in the PERF
DES page. Even if it has been entered by the flight crew, this entry
is still considered as a managed speed.
Manual Switching
When the speed/Mach mode is
selected, the flight crew can perform the switching, by pressing the  SPD/MACH  on the  FCU  ( ).

General
The  AP / FD
TCAS
mode is an  AP / FD  vertical mode, that provides vertical guidance in the case
of a  RA  alert, generated by the  TCAS .  When a  TA  is triggered, the  AP / FD
TCAS
mode arms.
When an  RA  is triggered,
the  AP / FD
TCAS
mode engages to provide guidance
in accordance with the  RA  order:
The  AP  status does not change: Remains engaged or disengaged
If not previously
engaged, the  FD s automatically engage.
When the "CLEAR OF CONFLICT"
aural alert sounds, the  AP / FD
TCAS
mode disengages.  The  AP / FD  provides guidance toward the latest
target altitude set on the  FCU .

EGPWS , WINDSHEAR, or STALL warning is not triggered.

or engage, the  AP / FD

Approach Overview
Flight guidance can perform different
types of approaches.  .
Approach Selection
Approach Selection
Standard Selection
The flight crew selects the approach
via the ARRIVAL page.
Approach Selection - Manual Tuning on FMS
Manual Tuning on the FMS
If the flight crew manually-tunes
an  LS  approach on the RADIO  NAV  page, the flight
guidance system will disregard the manual tuning and guide the aircraft
on the approach selected on the ARRIVAL page.
If the approach selected on
the ARRIVAL page and the  LS  approach set on the RADIO  NAV  page are different:
The manually-tuned  LS  approach on the RADIO  NAV  page is disregarded,
and the  CHECK APPR
SEL  message is displayed on the  FMA , and on the  MCDU  Scratchpad.
The aircraft
will fly the approach selected on the ARRIVAL page.
Approach Selection - Manual Tuning on FMS
Manual Tuning on the FMS
If the flight crew manually-tunes an  LS  approach on the RADIO  NAV  page, the flight guidance
system will guide the aircraft on the manually-tuned approach.
If the approach selected on
the ARRIVAL page and the  LS  approach set on the RADIO  NAV  page are different:
The approach
selected on the ARRIVAL page is disregarded, and the  CHECK APPR
SEL  message is displayed on the  FMA , and on the  MCDU  Scratchpad
The aircraft
will fly the manually-tuned  LS  approach on the RADIO  NAV  page.
Approach Selection - Manual Tuning on the RMP (backup)
Manual Tuning on the RMP (Backup)
If all the  FMC s are
fault, the flight crew selects the  NAV  key on the  RMP  1 or 2, in order to manually-tune the frequency, or select
a
GLS
approach, or an  ILS  approach.
Approach Selection - Selection in the MMRs
Selection in the  MMR s
When an approach is selected
on the ARRIVAL page, or manually-tuned on RADIO  NAV  page,
or via the  RMP , the approach frequency and course are sent
to both  MMR s.  In case of discrepancy between
both  MMR s the
NAV  LS TUNING DISAGREE
alert triggers.
Below  700
RA , when an approach mode is engaged, the flight guidance system freezes
the LS selection in the  MMR . As a result, the  MMR  does not take into account any change of the LS selection.
ILS Guidance Mode
ILS  Guidance Mode
An  ILS  guidance mode uses the Localizer and Glideslope
signals from localizer antennas and a glideslope antenna on ground.  The  MMR  computes
the  ILS  lateral and vertical angular deviations.  The  ILS  lateral deviation is referred to as the  LOC  deviation, and the  ILS  vertical deviation is referred
to as the  G/S  deviation.  The  FG  uses the  LOC  and  G/S  deviations in order to fly the aircraft along
the  LOC  and  G/S  beams.
Approach Modes
The  ILS  guidance
modes are:
Lateral Guidance
Vertical Guidance
Above  400
RA
LOC
* : Capture of the  LOC  beam
LOC  : Track of the  LOC  beam
G/S
* : Capture of the  G/S  beam
G/S  : Track of the  G/S  beam
Below  400
RA , and until end of roll out
LAND : Track of  LOC  and  G/S  beams
FLARE : Alignment of the yaw axis on the runway
centerline, and flare on the pitch axis
ROLL OUT : Track of the runway centerline,
and nose down
Approach and Landing Capability
In accordance with the approach minima
and the landing technique, minimum approach and landing capabilities
are required.
GLS  Guidance Mode
GLS
Guidance Mode
The  GLS  guidance mode uses
the  GNSS  position with a correction and integrity signal
from a ground station also known as  GBAS .  The  MMR  computes the  GLS  deviations.  The  GLS  lateral deviation
is referred to as the  LOC  deviation, and the  GLS  vertical deviation is referred to as the  G/S  deviation.
The computed lateral and vertical
deviations are available up to  20  from the runway
threshold.
The  FG  uses the  LOC  and  G/S  deviations in
order to fly the aircraft along the  LOC  and  G/S  approach path, like  ILS .
Approach Modes
The  GLS  guidance modes are:
Lateral Guidance
Vertical Guidance
Above  400
RA
LOC
* : Capture of the  LOC  beam
LOC  : Track of the  LOC  beam
G/S
* : Capture of the  G/S  beam
G/S  : Track of the  G/S  beam
Below  400
RA , and until end of roll out
LAND : Track of  LOC  and  G/S  beams
FLARE : Alignment of the yaw axis on the runway
centerline, and flare on the pitch axis
ROLL OUT : Track of the runway centerline,
and nose down
Approach and Landing Capability
In accordance with the approach minima
and the landing technique, minimum approach and landing capabilities
are required.
SLS  Guidance Mode
SLS
Guidance Mode
The  SLS  guidance mode uses
the  GNSS  position with a correction and integrity signal
from satellite constellations also known as  SBAS .  The  SLS  guidance mode enables the flight crew to fly an  RNAV  ( GNSS ) straight-in approach with LPV minima, or LP minima
with the  LOC  guidance mode only.  The  MMR  computes the  SLS  deviations.  The  SLS  lateral deviation
is referred to as the  LOC  deviation, and the  SLS  vertical deviation is referred to as the  G/S  deviation.  The  FG  uses the  LOC  and  G/S  deviations in
order to fly the aircraft along the  LOC  and  G/S  approach path, like  ILS .
Approach Modes
The  SLS  guidance modes are:
Lateral Guidance
Vertical Guidance
Above  400
RA
LOC
* : Capture of the  LOC  beam
LOC  : Track of the  LOC  beam
G/S
* : Capture of the  G/S  beam
G/S  : Track of the  G/S  beam
Below  400
RA
LAND : Track of  LOC  and  G/S  beams
FLARE : Alignment of the yaw axis on the runway
centerline, and flare on the pitch axis
ROLL OUT : Track of the runway centerline,
and nose down
Approach and Landing Capability
In accordance with the approach
minima and the landing technique, minimum approach and landing capabilities
are required.
Guidance Selection
Guidance Selection
The default guidance mode is
the  FLS  mode.  The flight crew can check/select
the appropriate guidance mode ( FLS  or FINAL  APP ) through the  PERF
APPR  page.
For RNAV(RNP), FINAL
APP must be selected.
FLS Function Availability
FLS  Function Availability
The  FLS  function
is available, if the flight crew selects:
A  VOR ,  RNAV ,  GNSS ,  LOC  or  LOC
B/C  approach on the ARRIVAL page
An  ILS  approach on the ARRIVAL page, and deselects the  G/S  on
the RADIO NAV page.
However, the  FLS  function
is not available, if:
The  MAP  is before the runway threshold, and
The difference
between the final approach course and the runway course is more than  50 .
If the  FLS  function is not available for an approach, the  NO FLS
FOR THIS APPR  message appears in the  MCDU  Scratchpad.

Fail Concept
FAIL-OPERATIONAL AUTOMATIC LANDING SYSTEM
An automatic landing system is fail-operational
if, in the event of a failure below alert height, the remaining part
of the automatic landing system allows the aircraft to complete the
approach, flare, and landing.  The  CAT3 DUAL  approach and landing
capability is fail-operational automatic landing system.
In the event of a
failure, the automatic landing system operates as a fail-passive system.
FAIL-PASSIVE AUTOMATIC LANDING SYSTEM
An automatic landing system
is fail-passive if, in the event of a failure, there is no significant
out-of-trim condition, or deviation of flight path or attitude, but
the landing is not completed automatically.
The following approach and landing
capabilities are fail-passive automatic landing system.
CAT3 SINGLE
CAT2
CAT1
With a fail-passive automatic
landing system, the flight crew controls the aircraft after a failure.

is displayed in the "Approach and Landing Capability" column
of the  FMA  and of the

HDG/TRK Preset
General
The system has a  HDG / TRK  preset function for takeoff and go-around.  If the flight crew decides not to fly
the flight plan after takeoff or go-around, the flight crew can turn
the
HDG/TRK
on the  FCU  to preset a heading
or a track. The set value remains displayed in the  FCU
HDG / TRK  window until the flight crew pulls the knob.
At takeoff
If the flight crew presets the  HDG / TRK  before takeoff and up to  30
RA ,
NAV
disarms.
The preset value remains displayed in the  HDG / TRK  window (even when
RWY
TRK
engages at  30
RA ).  When the flight crew pulls the  HDG/TRK  (at least  5  after liftoff),
HDG
or  TRACK  mode engages.  The aircraft follows the preset target.
HDG/TRK Preset
At Go-Around
If the flight crew presets the  HDG / TRK  when
LOC
* ,
LOC  ,
LOC
B/C  ,
LOC
B/C
* ,
F-LOC
*  ,
F-LOC
,  LAND ,  FLARE ,  ROLL OUT  or
GA
TRK
mode is engaged, the preset value
remains displayed in the  HDG / TRK  window, as
long as one of theses modes is engaged.  After go-around engagement,
HDG  / TRACK  will engage, when the flight crew pulls
the  HDG/TRK .  When the
HDG

Engine Operations on Ground in Icing Conditions
INTRODUCTION
During engine operations
on ground in icing conditions, and with  OAT  at  +3  ( 37 ) or below, ice accretion may affect
the engine fan blades, spinner, or stators of the low pressure compressor.
Apply the following
engine ice shedding procedure to prevent possible engine degradation
or damage.
The quantity of ice accretion depends on the time during which the
engine is running on ground in the above mentioned icing conditions.
This procedure involves the performance of engine accelerations before
the end of specific time intervals, or if the engine vibrations increase
during taxi.
PRELIMINARY COCKPIT PREPARATION
If the engines are operated on ground in icing conditions with  OAT  at  +3  ( 37 ) or below:
LOGBOOK  CHECK
Check the taxi-in time of the
previous flight in icing conditions with  OAT  at  +3  ( 37 ) or below recorded in the logbook.

NEXT ENGINE ACCELERATION  DETERMINE

in the logbook

taxi-in time of the previous flight, if a maintenance task to deice
the engines is performed before engine start.

Engine Operations on Ground in Icing Conditions
INTRODUCTION
During engine operations
on ground in icing conditions and with  OAT  at  +3  ( 37 ) or below, ice accretion may affect
the engine fan blades, spinner or stators of the low pressure compressor.
Apply the following
procedure for engine ice shedding to prevent possible engine degradation
or damage.
The quantity of ice accretion depends
on the time during which the engines are running on ground in the
above-mentioned icing conditions.
This procedure requires the
acceleration of the engines:
Before the end
of specific time intervals,
If the engine
vibrations increase during taxi,
Before takeoff.
The taxi-out time starts when the first
engine is running, and finishes when the aircraft is lined up on the
departure runway for takeoff. The taxi-in time starts at touchdown,
and finishes when the flight crew shuts down both engines.  The flight crew may refer to the following
diagram to anticipate the procedure that must be performed during
the taxi-out.  The flight crew must refer to the procedure
for engine ice shedding in addition to the  SOP s.  the following procedure .
Procedure for Engine Ice Shedding
If in icing conditions and with  OAT  at  3  ( 37 ) or below:
During the following
procedure, the flight crew must use visibility only (and not  RVR ).
If at any time during
the operation of the engines on ground there is  FZFG  and
the visibility is lower than  150  ( 500 ), the takeoff is not authorized and a maintenance action is due.
With  FZFG  and visibility lower than  150  ( 500 ):
TAKEOFF  NOT AUTHORIZED
With  FZFG  and visibility equal to or higher than  150  ( 500 ), or without  FZFG :

time of the previous flight

task to deice the engines is performed before engine start, disregard
the taxi-in time of the previous flight and the running time of the

action is due.

Erroneous Display of ACTIVE ATC ICAO Code on the DCDU and MCDU
DESCRIPTION
Following a transition from an European  ATN  B1 or B2  ATC  center ( ACTIVE ATC , e.g. EISN) to a North Atlantic  FANS  1/A  ATC  center ( NEXT ATC , e.g. EGGX), an abnormal disconnection
of the  CPDLC  may occur. The flight crew can connect again
to the first North Atlantic  FANS  1/A  ATC  center
(e.g. EGGX). After an automatic transfer to the next  ATC  center (e.g. CZQX), the flight crew can detect an erroneous  DCDU  and  MCDU  display of the  ACTIVE ATC
ICAO  code.  The  DCDU  and the  MCDU  may still display the first  FANS  1/A  ATC  center
(e.g. EGGX) as the  ACTIVE
ATC , even if the  CPDLC  connection is established
and active with the controlling  FANS  1/A  ATC  center (e.g. CZQX).  The content of the  CPDLC  messages is not modified. The  CPDLC  message is transmitted
to or received from the controlling  ATC  center (e.g. CZQX).
Only the display of the  ACTIVE
ATC
ICAO  code on the  DCDU  and the  MCDU  is erroneous (e.g. EGGX instead of CZQX).  This behavior may occur after a transition from the European airspace
toward the North Atlantic airspace.
OPERATIONAL RECOMMENDATIONS
In the case of an erroneous
display of the  ACTIVE
ATC
ICAO  code on the  DCDU  and on the  MCDU , the flight crew can perform one of the following actions:
When the conditions
permit, the flight crew should inform by voice the controlling  ATC  center and then disconnect all  ATC  centers on
the CONNECTION STATUS page of the  MCDU . Then, the flight
crew can notify the controlling  ATC  center on the NOTIFICATION
page, or
If the previous
action is not possible, or the new  CPDLC  connection with  ATC  is not established (no  ACTIVE ATC  on the  DCDU ), the flight
crew must revert to voice communication and notify  ATC .

CLB Mode Engagement After Takeoff With QFE Setting
DESCRIPTION
FMS design
During takeoff roll, at  90 , the  FMS
TO  phase engages. At the  FMS
TO  phase engagement, the  FMS  checks that the  FCU  altitude displayed on the  FCU  altitude window
is above the following altitudes displayed on the  FMS
PERF
TO  page:
THR
RED  altitude, and
ACC  altitude.
If the  FCU  value
displayed on the  FCU  altitude window is:
Below the  THR
RED  altitude, then the  THR
RED  altitude is set to the maximum value between the  FCU  value
and the airport altitude +  400
Below the  ACC  altitude, then the  ACC  altitude is set to the
maximum value between the  FCU  value and the airport altitude
+  400 .
If the  THR
RED  /  ACC  altitudes are updated,
the  FMS
PERF
TO  page is updated accordingly.
Abnormal behavior
An anomaly exists when using the  QFE  setting.
In the above mentioned logic, the value displayed in the  FCU  altitude window is considered as an altitude despite the  QFE  setting.
Therefore, in the case of the  QFE  setting,
the logic compares an height (value displayed in the  FCU  altitude window) with an altitude ( THR
RED  /
ACC  altitudes displayed on the  FMS
TO
PERF  page that are  QNH  referenced).
As a consequence, depending
on the conditions, the value displayed in the  FCU  altitude
window ( QFE  setting) may be lower than the  THR
RED  /  ACC  altitude ( QNH  setting),
and all of the following occur:
At  FMS
TO  phase activation, the  THR
RED  /  ACC  altitudes are updated and set below the expected
ones with a minimum possible value at airport altitude +  400
The  FMS
PERF
TO  page is updated accordingly
The autoflight system acts as
per design. When the aircraft reaches:
The updated  THR
RED  altitude, then:
LVR
CLB
flashes
CLB
engages
FMS
PERF
CLB  page replaces the  FMS
PERF
TO  page.
The updated  ACC  altitude, then the aircraft accelerates to the
CLB
managed speed target.
In the case of  OEI , when the aircraft is above the updated  THR
RED  /  ACC  altitude, the flight crew should set  TOGA  thrust to recover
SRS  . The  FMS  go-around phase activates.
OPERATIONAL RECOMMENDATIONS
In the case of  QFE  operation, during the flight preparation, the flight crew may identify
that, at least one of the following values, is higher than the value
displayed in the  FCU  altitude window:
The  THR
RED  value displayed on the  FMS
PERF
TO  page, or
The  ACC  value displayed on the  FMS
PERF
TO  Page.
For this comparison, the flight
crew should consider the values without  QNH / QFE  conversion, as described in the illustration above.
Then, the flight crew
should proceed as follows:
Request for
a higher  ATC  clearance height. This higher  ATC  clearance height should be at least the maximum value between the  THR
RED  altitude and the  ACC  altitude
displayed on the  FMS
PERF
TO  page,
without considering  QNH / QFE  conversion.
If the  ATC  is not in position to provide a higher  ATC  clearance
height, the flight crew should request to operate in  QNH .

can be fulfilled, the flight crew should apply all of the following
during the takeoff climb path:

Disregard
LVR
CLB
flashing on  FMA  and

THR
CLB
engages

In the case of  OEI  above the not expected early

SRS

Loss of FMS Predictions in Low Density of Airports
Description
The  FMS  may encounter
temporary and repetitive loss of predictions in the flight plan of
the  MCDU  during flight, if the  FMS  finds only
4 airports in the Navigation Database within  1200  from the
aircraft position.  The occurrence
rate increases when the flight crew enters a 5th airport on [5L] key
of the CLOSEST AIRPORTS page.
During the occurrence, the  UTC  fields of the 4th and 5th (when entered) airports are dashed
in the CLOSEST AIRPORTS page.
Operational Recommendation
The flight
crew should clear the 5th airport in the CLOSEST AIRPORTS page to
recover the full  FMS  predictions.  To avoid new occurrences in flight, the operator should request the  FMS  supplier to modify the Navigation Database to increase
the number of available airports, on the flight routes affected by
the loss of predictions. A minimum of 5 airports must be available
within  1200  of all expected flight plans.

General
Two types of  MCDU  messages exist:
Type I: Direct
result of a flight crew action
Type II: Information
about a situation, or an action request to the flight crew.
Type II messages are stored
in a first-in/first-out message queue (5 messages maximum).  They are suppressed, if correct data is entered, or when they no
longer apply.  The flight crew can clear all
messages by pressing the  CLR  key on the  MCDU  console.

Erroneous Selection
of FINAL APP instead of FLS on Ground
Description
The following
misbehavior is reported on aircraft equipped with  FLS /FINAL
APP coexistence.
On ground before the takeoff,
the  FMS  erroneously selects FINAL APP guidance instead
of FLS guidance when all the following occurs:
The flight plan
contains a departure runway
The flight crew
selects an  RNAV  ( GNSS ) approach with  LNAV  minima or with  LNAV / VNAV  minima
The flight crew
selects a  STAR  with a VIA.
Following
the insertion of the APPROACH and  STAR  in the ACTIVE flight
plan, the PERF APPR page displays  FINAL APP  selected instead of
FLS
selected.  In flight, when the flight crew arms
the approach, the FINAL APP guidance arms.
Operational Recommendation
After
insertion on ground of an  RNAV  approach with a  STAR  and a VIA, the flight crew must check the selected guidance on the
PERF APPR page. Reselect  FLS  as required.  As per the  SOP  Approach using  F-LOC
F-G/S  guidance, CHECK/SELECT FLS on PERF APPR page during the descent
preparation.

One Engine Taxi At
Arrival
No less than  3  after high thrust operations:
COOLING TIME ELAPSED  ANNOUNCE
The flight crew should operate
the engines at or near idle thrust for a cooling period of  3  before engine shutdown, in order to thermally stabilize
the engines.
Idle reverse thrust and normal
thrust to maneuver during taxi (i.e. at or near idle), are not considered
as high thrust operations. Therefore, both of the following applies:
If the flight
crew used idle reverse thrust for landing and normal thrust to maneuver
during taxi after landing, the cooling period starts when the flight
crew retards the thrust lever during the flare
If the flight
crew used maximum reverse thrust for landing, the cooling period starts
when the flight crew sets the thrust lever to idle reverse during
the landing rollout.
Before engine shutdown,
routine cooling periods that last less than the recommended time,
can result in engine degradation.
When taxiing in a straight line:
ENG 2 SHUTDOWN  ORDER
During engine shutdown, a slight
jerk forward may occur if the brakes are applied while the aircraft
is moving.

down Engine 2, they must check that the  AVAIL  light of the  APU START  is on.

CIDS
CABIN READY
This memo indicates to the flight
crew that the cabin is ready for take-off or for landing. This memo
appears when the cabin crew presses the 'CABIN READY' key
on the  FAP .
The  CABIN READY  memo is displayed on the right
side of the memos area or in the  T/O  and  LDG  memos checklist depending on the  CIDS  standard and customisation.
CABIN...CHECK
This memo appears in the  T/O  and  LDG  memos checklist and indicates that the
cabin is not ready for take-off or for landing ('CABIN READY' key
not selected on the
FAP  ).
Controls and Indicators
Controls
The flight crew cannot deactivate the  ALTSM  function.
PFD  indication
In the case of an erroneous setting of
the barometric altitude, the  QNH  or the
QFE
value becomes amber and flashes on both  PFD s. Then  9  after an “ALTIMETER SETTING”
aural alert is emitted.
The barometric
altitude value also  flashes on the
HUD s .
General
The  ALTSM  function provides
an awareness of an erroneous setting of the barometric reference,
during departure or arrival, while operating between  600
RA  and  6000
AAL . This function
uses  QNH  or
QFE
settings.

Wing Tank Fuel Quantity Indication
WING TANK FUEL QUANTITY INDICATION
The fuel quantity in the wing tank is within a normal range.  Appears in multiples
of  10  ( 20 ).  Pulses in green in
flight phase 2 and 6 when the difference between the fuel quantities
in the two wings is more than  1500  ( 3300 ). The pulse occurs on the highest fuel quantity tank.
The values accuracy is degraded.
For more information,  .
The wing tank overflows.
The fuel quantity indication is not valid.
Center Tank Fuel Quantity Indication
CENTER TANK FUEL QUANTITY INDICATION
The fuel quantity in the center tank is within a normal range.  Appears in multiples
of  10  ( 20 ).
The value accuracy is degraded.  For more information,  .
Center tank fuel is partially unusable.
The fuel quantity indication is not valid.

Erroneous Mach Target Indicator on the PFD
Description
When the flight crew uses the  DBUS , the backup Mach target on the right side of the speed tape is erroneous.
Meanwhile, the backup Mach displayed below the speed tape remains
reliable and provides the current backup Mach as estimated by the
speed monitoring function.  .
Operational Recommendations
When  DBUS  is used, do not
use Mach target mode ( SPD/MACH  on the  FCU ).
Even at an altitude higher than the crossover altitude, the flight
crew should keep the speed target mode and monitor the Mach via the
backup Mach indication provided below the speed tape.

Noises that May Result in the Loss of Audio Communications
DESCRIPTION
Specific noises (crackling, horn, etc.)
can be identified via the Captain ( F/O ) (3rd occupant)
boomset and/or the Captain ( F/O ) loudspeaker. The noise
may increase until all communications are no longer audible.  The horn noise may be generated at  RMP  power-up. It is a loud acoustic feedback that may be heard
when the flight crew listen to the interphone at a high volume.
OPERATIONAL RECOMMENDATION
In the case of specific noises, the flight
crew should first reduce the volume of the interphone.  Then, the flight crew should reset the  RMP  connected to the boomset, or loudspeaker from which the
noise could be identified, via the following actions:
Set the  RMP  BRT/OFF knob to the OFF position
Wait  5
Set the INT
reception knob to the minimum audible level
Set the  RMP  BRT/OFF knob to the appropriate BRT position
Adjust the volume
via the INT reception knob as required.
If the
reset is not successful, the flight crew should switch off the identified
affected  RMP . As a result, the following occurs:
If the  RMP  1(2) is
switched off:
There is an
automatic reconfiguration of the audio system on the
ACP  3 (  RMP  3 )
The loudspeaker
and the hand microphone on the affected side become inoperative
On the affected
side, the flight crew should use a boomset.
If the
RMP  3  is switched off, the communication
between the cockpit and the ground crew is lost.

Inadvertent T.O. Data Reversion Upon RWY Change
Description
In the
case of a runway change, the  FMS  may erroneously revert
to the previous takeoff speeds and takeoff thrust (FLX TO or  DRT TO ) when all the following occurs:
Both  MCDU s display the  PERF  TAKEOFF page,
V1,
VR and V2 associated with the previous runway are already entered,
The
new runway is entered in one  MCDU ,
V1,
VR and V2 associated with the new runway are entered by one flight
crew member,
The other flight
crew member presses the 6R prompt (NEXT PHASE or CONFIRM TO DATA)
of the  PERF  TAKEOFF page.
Operational Recommendations
If the  PERF  TAKEOFF page is displayed on both  MCDU s, when
the new takeoff speeds are entered on one  MCDU , the flight
crew should not press the 6R prompt (NEXT PHASE or CONFIRM TO DATA)
on the other  MCDU .  The flight
crew should apply the DEPARTURE CHANGE SOP and complete the DEPARTURE
CHANGE checklist to ensure that correct speeds and thrust are set
for the takeoff.

Taxi - Radar
Weather Radar
RADAR  ON
To check the departure path,
set the  TILT  to  MAN . The flight crew can then
set the radar to the  AUTO  position.
PREDICTIVE
WINDSHEAR SYSTEM
AUTO
When the  MULTISCAN  is
in the AUTO position (tilt in automatic mode) and the GAIN is set
to CAL (automatically calibrated), the radar display may not entirely
correspond to the current weather. Therefore, this Temporary DU is
issued to indicate that, when the  MULTISCAN  is in the AUTO
position, the GAIN should be manually set to +8 to ensure that the
radar display provides an optimum reflection of the current weather
condition.
In addition, the flight crew
should temporarily set the  MULTISCAN  to MAN, if:
The weather
is good, or not significant, in order to check that the radar is operating
correctly
The weather
display is ambiguous or unexpected, in order to better analyze the
weather situation.
When the  MULTISCAN  is
in the AUTO position and the GAIN is manually set, the Path Attenuation
Compensation (PAC) alert is not available. However, the radar display
corresponds to the current weather conditions, when the aircraft is
above  150 .
Therefore, the flight crew can
set the GAIN back to CAL, when the aircraft is above  150 .
Taxi - Radar
Weather Radar
RADAR  ON
To check the departure path,
set the  MULTISCAN  to  MAN . The flight crew can
then set the radar to the  AUTO  position.  Gain must be manually set to
+8, when  MULTISCAN  is set to  AUTO  and when flying
below  150 .
The flight crew monitors the
weather radar display in  AUTO  mode, and confirms any weather
display that is ambiguous or unexpected using manual tilt according
to standard techniques.
PREDICTIVE
WINDSHEAR SYSTEM
AUTO
When in the AUTO position, the
MultiScan AUTO mode adjusts the tilt according to the altitude of
the aircraft.  In cruise, MULTISCAN function
provides a large view of the weather ahead, ie display of weather
cells located on and below aircraft path.  At low altitudes (below  200 ), the tilt is adjusted upward
to manage clutter from strong ground targets. In some cases, the weather
may be low-lying and therefore may be below the radar beam and not
be displayed until the aircraft descends closer to the precipitation
level.  Therefore, this Temporary Revision
is issued to indicate that, when the Multiscan is in the AUTO position,
the GAIN should be manually set to +4 when the aircraft is below  200 .
In addition, the flight crew
should temporarily set the  MULTISCAN  to MAN, if:
If the weather
is good, or not significant, in order to check that the radar is operating
correctly: down tilt until displaying ground echoes
The weather
display is ambiguous or unexpected, in order to better analyze the
weather situation using manual tilt according to standard technique
In particular
below  200 , for situations with low-level weather, weather
with low reflectivity or in front of suspected active cells, the flight
crew should switch to Manual mode and adjust the tilt setting downward
until the weather is detected or the ground clutter appears on the
upper part of the display.
In addition, the flight crew
may increase the manual gain control to display lower reflectivity
targets. The manual gain control can be increased in both AUTO and
Manual modes to display lower levels of weather.  In both cases, ground
clutter may also be displayed as a result of low settings and/or increased
gain.
