due to ACT F-PLN corruption by SEC F-PLN
Description
An  FMS  misbehavior can occur due to a spurious data exchange between
the secondary flight plan and the active flight plan, with the following
effects on one  FMS  only:
Erroneous distances
computation
Erroneous  ETA  and  EFOB  values.
The fuel
predictions discrepancy between both  MCDU s may increase
with time. When the erroneous  EFOB  at destination is below
the specified minimum, the  FMS  triggers the  DEST EFOB BELOW MIN  scratchpad
message.  This malfunction can disappear spontaneously
upon  F-PLN  recomputation.  This misbehavior
may occur in one of the following situations:
The crew performs
a  COPY ACTIVE  and changes the  SEC  destination to an alternate airport, and an offset is inserted in
the active  F-PLN , or
The crew performs
a  COPY ACTIVE  and changes the  SEC  destination to the departure airport.
Operational Recommendation
If the crew observes the effects
detailed above (erroneous distances, time to destination and fuel
predictions on one  MCDU ), and confirms that there is no
fuel leak, they should perform the following actions:
On  SEC  index, press  DELETE SEC  prompt.
On  PROG  index, re-enter the  CRZ
FL  in
order to recompute active  F-PLN  predictions.

GPS Interference - Introduction
The flight crew can anticipate
the risk of  GPS  interference via the presence of  NOTAM s (from Authority or Company).  When the flight crew suspects  GPS  interference due to the cockpit effects, the flight crew can check
the  GPS  data. The  FMS  page GPS MONITOR may display
dashes or erroneous data on  GPS  positions, and/or the number
of tracked satellites ("MODE/SAT") may be lower than 5 or
null, in the case of  GPS  interference.
In the absence of data available
(dashed) in the GPS MONITOR page, the flight crew should consider
the  GPS  capability of the affected equipment inoperative.
Depending on the number of  GPS  impacted, the aircraft condition
may no longer be compliant with the minimum navigation equipment required
for  RNP  operations.

General Information
The Airbus policy about the crew resource
management includes three cases : PF or PM, PF-PM or BOTH.
PF or PM
PF or PM is used for individual
actions. The actions should be completed by a single crew member,
the PF or the PM. This rule also applies for CM1 or CM2.
PF-PM
PF-PM means that the PF and
the PM perform the same action, but not necessarily simultaneously.
This rule also applies for CM1-CM2.
BOTH
BOTH means both pilots are doing
the same action at the same time, because there is a need to coordinate
or share what is done.

GPS Interference - Parking - All
PARKING - IRS Performance
In the case of  GPS  spoofing,
if  FMS  position is affected, the POSITION MONITOR page
may provide erroneous  IRS  drift resulting in undue  ADIRU  removals.
The IRS MONITOR page provides data independent
from  GPS .
The data provided
by the IRS MONITOR page are based on flight plan data (destination
airport and runway).
GPS  deselection on the  FMS  before spoofing exposure would
prevent abnormal  IRS  drift display on
the POSITION/MONITOR page.
In the case of abnormal  IRS  drift observed on the
POSITION MONITOR page, the following procedure is recommended:
IRS PERFORMANCE  CHECK
On the IRS MONITOR
page, record the drift rate of  IRS  1,  IRS  2
and  IRS  3
Calculate the
block time of the  IRS
The block time of the  IRS  is equal to the accumulated block times, for each flight performed,
since last  IRS  alignment.
Multiply the
block time by the recorded drift rate
Compare the
result with table provided in  .
PARKING - LOGBOOK
The flight crew must report
any kind of interference encountered in flight as maintenance actions
may be required before the next flight.  If the maintenance actions are not performed, persistent effects
may remain on the aircraft.  for more information about the list of persistent effects.

Landscape Camera
The landscape camera system consists
of two cameras installed forward of the nose landing gear. These cameras
provide images that are displayed on the passenger entertainment system.
There is one forward-looking camera, and one down-looking camera.
By default, the forward-looking camera is used on ground, and the
down-looking camera is used in flight. However, the cabin crew is
able to manually select the camera.
Controls and Indicators On Overhead Panel
OFF
The landscape camera is not active.
The landscape camera is active.
On ground, the
landscape pictures are provided by the forward-looking camera.
In flight, the
landscape pictures are provided by the down-looking camera, when the
landing gear is up and locked.
OVRD PB
The  OVRD  function is not active.
The  OVRD  function is active. The passenger video program
is paused and replaced by the active landscape camera signal.
The OVRD function can be activated
only if the landscape camera is on.

Message Timers
Technical Timer
When the flight crew sends a
downlink message, a timer is started to ensure the successful delivery
of the message. If the ground does not confirm the good reception
of the message in time or the transmission of the message takes too
long, the message delivery is considered failed and  SEND FAILED  is displayed on the message information
area.
Message Timers
Technical Timer
When the flight crew sends a
downlink message, a timer is started to ensure the successful delivery
of the message. If the ground does not confirm the good reception
of the message in time or the transmission of the message takes too
long, the message delivery is considered failed and  SEND FAILED  is displayed on the message information
area.
Operational Response Timer
Operational response timers are used
in order to avoid datalink dialogues to remain open for too long.  When the  ATC  sends an uplink
message, the flight crew has  100  to answer. If the flight
crew needs more time to process the message and provide an answer,
they should answer STBY, in order to reset the operational response
timer. If the flight crew does not answer in time, the dialogue is
closed and  REPLY:
TIME OUT  is displayed on the message information area. The
flight crew should revert to voice communication to provide an answer
to the  ATC .
The  DCDU  displays  XX S FOR REPLY , on the message
information area,  30  before the expiration
of the operational response timer. This message informs the flight
crew about the time that remains until the timer expires.
When the
flight crew sends a downlink message that requires an answer from
the  ATC , the answer from the  ATC  must be received
within  4
30  ( 270 ).
If the  ATC  does not answer in time, the dialogue is closed
and  NO ATC REPLY  is displayed
on the message information area. The flight crew should revert to
voice communication to clarify the message status.

received within  7
30 . If

General
The following warnings and cautions
appear in the lower part of the  E/WD  if the aircraft is
not in takeoff configuration when the flight crew presses the  T.O CONFIG  on the  ECAM  control panel or applies
takeoff power.
How to change the paper roll
In order to change the paper
roll of the printer, the flight crew should apply the following procedure:
STEP 1
Release the locking system and lift the
door.
Remove the remaining paper from
the paper cutter.  Move the
paper mandrel to disengage it from its base.
STEP 2
Take a new paper roll.
Make sure that the edge of the paper
has a smooth cut, that the paper is free of creases and is rolled
tight.
Remove the empty paper roll and replace it with the new one.
Re-engage the paper mandrel into its initial position.
STEP 3
Feed the paper under the black roller
and through the slot of the paper cutter in the indicated direction.
Make sure that the paper is held firmly in position.
STEP 4
Close and lock the door.
Verify that the latch is engaged by pulling
the door handle outward.
To confirm that the printer
is ready for subsequent printing operations, press on the  SLEW  and check that the paper comes out correctly.
How to solve a paper jam
In the case of a confirmed paper jam,
the flight crew should apply the following procedure:
If the paper can be grasp:
Pull the paper with two hands until the printer releases the paper.
Pull the paper off.
Release the locking system and lift the door.  Close and lock the door.
If the paper cannot be grasp:
Release the locking system and lift the door.  Remove all the paper from the mechanical block and ensure that the
paper is flat.  Feed the paper under the black roller
and through the slot of the paper cutter in the direction indicated
on the self-adhesive labels.  Pull the paper until the paper is free of creases.  Close and lock the door.  Remove the creased paper with the paper cutter.
To confirm that the printer is ready for subsequent printing operations,
press on the  SLEW  and check that the paper comes out correctly.
GPS Interference
- Before the Interference Area
BEFORE THE INTERFERENCE AREA
In order to maintain most  ATC  datalink applications and the  FMS  predictions,
the flight crew should apply the following:
CLOCK  INT
When the clock is in INT mode:
The  ADS-C  application is considered as not available.  The Figure of Merit of the  ADS-C  reports will indicate a loss of the navigation accuracy,
that impacts the  PBCS  capability of the aircraft.
If the clock
was previously synchronized with the  GNSS , the INT mode
of the clock maintains all other  ATC  datalink applications
for  24 .
Setting the
clock to INT mode might not prevent erroneous  FMS  time
predictions in all cases.
GPS Interference
- Within the Interference Area - GPS clock
If the flight crew encounters unexpected  GPS  interference:
During the flight, the flight crew may suspect not anticipated  GPS  interference. In order to maintain the  FMS  predictions,
the flight crew should crosscheck the aircraft time with an external
reference.
ATC  TIME CHECK
The flight crew crosschecks
the external time reference with the aircraft clock.
If the external time is different from the time displayed on
the clock:
CLOCK  SET
Manually enter the time data
on the clock, based on the external time reference.
CLOCK  INT
When the clock is
switched to INT mode after manual entry in SET mode, the flight crew
should consider that the  ATC  datalink  CPDLC  and  ADS-C  applications are unavailable ( ).  The Figure of Merit of the  ADS-C  reports will indicate a loss of navigation accuracy,
that impacts the  PBCS  capability of the aircraft.
GPS Interference
- AFTER the Interference Area - GPS clock
If  GPS 1  data are confirmed reliable:
CLOCK  GPS
The clock should remain on INT
mode until the  GPS 1  NAV  mode is recovered.

Introduction
The flight crew should apply
the following procedures when the  QFE  is used as the barometric
reference at the departure and/or destination airport. It must be
used as an additional or amended part of the  SOP s for  QFE  operations.
Design Specificities
This section highlights design
specificities related to the use of the  QFE  during operations
on the following aircraft systems:
PFD
ND
MCDU .
EFIS Control Panel
At the  EFIS
CP  power-up, the barometric reference is  QFE , and
the  QFE  value is set to  1013  or  29.92  by default, depending on the selected barometric unit.
For more information on the
setting of the barometric reference through the  EFIS
CP :
.
EFIS and MCDU Displays
When the  QFE  reference
is selected on the  EFIS
CP , altitudes displayed
on the  PFD ,  ND  and  MCDU  do not have
the same barometric reference:
The  PFD  displays target altitudes that use the  QFE  barometric
reference ( AGL )
When below the
Transition Altitude:
The  MCDU  displays altitude predictions and altitude constraints that use
the  QNH  barometric reference ( AMSL ).
The  ND  displays altitude constraints that use the  QNH  barometric
reference ( AMSL ).
When above the
Transition Altitude, and independently of the  FCU  setting:
The  MCDU  displays altitude predictions and altitude constraints that use
the “ STD ” barometric reference ( FL ).
The  ND  displays altitude constraints that use the “ STD ” barometric
reference ( FL ).

FMGS Preparation - QNH at Destination Pre-Entry (PERF/APPR

PERF APPR QNH field  INSERT
The  QNH  at destination can be obtained from the meteorological information
available before departure. If meteorological information provides
the  QFE , the flight crew must convert the  QFE  value to the  QNH  value.
During  QFE  Operations, the flight crew must enter a  QNH  (not a  QFE ) in the PERF APPR page. The  CPC  uses the  QNH  to compute the cabin pressurization profile. Therefore,
the entry of  QFE  in  QNH  field of the PERF APPR
page leads to an erroneous cabin pressurization profile.

When the aircraft approaches the transition level, and when

BAROMETRIC REFERENCE  SET/CROSSCHECK

The flight crew

If required, the  QFE  value must be converted to the  QNH  for the entry on the FMS PERF APPR page.
The flight crew
should pay attention to a barometric reference that significantly
differs from the one used for approach preparation. That could be
the symptom of a barometric reference error. In this case, the flight
crew should consider the confirmation of the barometric reference
from all available sources.
During  QFE  operations, the flight crew must convert  QFE  into  QNH . The  CPC  uses the  QNH  to compute
the cabin pressurization profile. Therefore, the entry of  QFE  in  QNH  field of the PERF APPR page leads to an erroneous
cabin pressurization profile.

Protective Breathing Equipment ( PBE )
GENERAL
The Protective Breathing Equipment ( PBE ) protects the eyes and respiratory system of the user from
toxic fumes, gases and smoke. Different models of  PBE s
can be installed in the aircraft.
DESCRIPTION
Each  PBE  model has:
An oxygen generator
that supplies oxygen to the  PBE  for 15 minutes
A mechanism
to initiate oxygen flow
A visor and
a hood
A neck seal:
To prevent oxygen
leakage from outside the  PBE , and
To keep fumes,
gases and smoke out of the  PBE .
An optional
mouthpiece (speech transmitter) and/or valve to help:
Breathing, and/or
Communication.
An optional
body belt.
LOCATION
The  PBE  is installed in several
areas in the cabin and in the cockpit.  .
STOWAGE
Each  PBE  is stowed
in a vacuum sealed or moisture resistant bag that is then stowed in
a protective container.

Introduction
The vertical flight plan is
divided into flight phases. For each phase, the  FMS  computes
the optimum speed or Mach Profile. These flight phases are:  Preflight - Takeoff - Climb - Cruise - Descent - Approach - Go-Around
- Done.

The  FMS  vertical profile does not take into account the effect of low  OAT . Therefore, vertical managed guidance:
Must not be
used when the actual  OAT  is below the minimum temperature
indicated on the approach chart or defined by the Operator, or
May not be used
when temperature corrections are required ( FINAL APP  mode may not engage).

wind is within limits

Approach using FINAL
APP Guidance for RNP(VPT) - General
General
RNP (VPT) are instrument
flight procedures composed of an instrument path followed by a visual
path defined by waypoints.  On the visual path, the aircraft navigates
using the  RNAV  system, but the position is monitored by
visual references to the ground, obstacle and other traffic.
RNP (VPT) approach must be stored and retrievable from
the Navigation Database.  In addition, the following items are
to be performed in the case of  RNP (VPT) approaches using
FINAL APP.  The procedures of the paragraph below are generic guidelines for  RNP (VPT) approaches. These procedures may be tailored by the
airline for specific airfields according to their  OPS  approval.
Approach using FINAL

Aircraft Equipment

One  MCDU

Two  FCU  channels
1  GPS  or 1  DME  receiver to update  FM  position
Additional requirement if indicated
on the approach chart.

APP Guidance for RNP(VPT) - Management of Degraded Navigation
Management of Degraded Navigation
Before the Visual Fix:
Discontinue the approach in
the following cases, if external visual references are not sufficient
to proceed visually:
NAV  FM/GPS POS DISAGREE
GPS PRIMARY LOST  on both NDs
After the Visual Fix
In the following cases, revert
to  TRK-FPA :
XTK
>  1  RNP
NAV  FM/GPS POS DISAGREE
NAV ACCUR DOWNGRAD  on both NDs
The use of the  AP  and  FD  is at the discretion
of the flight crew.  The decision to go-around is at the discretion of the flight crew
depending on the circumstances.

radar is not affected by GPS spoofing.

How to Use the PBE
PREFLIGHT CHECK
The  PBE  is stowed
in a container that enables the flight crew to perform the preflight
check via a condition indicator, serviceability indicator or humidity
indicator via an observation window. Some  PBE  containers
have a tamper seal or tamper latch to indicate if the container was
opened. In the case the tamper seal or tamper latch is broken, immediately
inform the maintenance team.  It is the responsibility of
the operator to define the preflight checks in accordance with the
manufacturers guidelines and local regulations. Preflight checks of
the  PBE  may include:
The location
is correct
The quantity
is correct
Check the condition,
serviceability or humidity Indicator
The tamper seal
or tamper latch is intact
The equipment
is secured
The expiration
date of the equipment is not expired
The general
condition of the container.
REMOVAL FROM CONTAINER AND VACUUM OR MOISTURE RESISTANT BAG
The  PBE  must be removed
from the container and from the vacuum/moisture resistant bag in accordance
with the instructions of the manufacturer.
Force may be required
to break the seal and/or bracket of the container.
To remove the  PBE  from the vacuum/moisture resistant bag, the user must pull the ‘tear-off
strips’, or where indicated on the bag. More than one ‘tear-off strip’
may be installed.
Ensure hands are dry to open
the vacuum/moisture resistant bag.
When removed from the vacuum/moisture
resistant bag, the  PBE  must be unfolded. The  PBE  must be unfolded in accordance with the instructions of the manufacturer
to prevent damage to the device.
HOW TO DON THE  PBE
The user must don the  PBE  away from fire/flames.  The  PBE  neck seal
must be widened to be able to don the  PBE  in accordance
with the instructions of the manufacturer. The neck seal of the  PBE  is tight, in order to keep any smoke, gases or fumes out
of the hood of the  PBE .  The hair of the user must be fully in the hood, if not, this may
enable outside air to enter the  PBE .
If the neck seal is damaged, the  PBE  must be replaced.
Users who wear glasses
should refer to the documentation of the manufacturer for guidance
to don the  PBE .
Make sure all hair
is in the neck seal/hood so that there is an entire seal around the
neck.
OXYGEN ACTIVATION
The oxygen supply of the  PBE  is activated before, during or after the user dons the  PBE .
When the
oxygen supply is activated, there may be a noise due to the oxygen
that flows inside the hood. The noise may disappear after this initial
phase depending on the  PBE  model.  When the oxygen supply is activated, the oxygen flow cannot be stopped.
The user should be aware of the time when the oxygen is activated,
and check the time of when the oxygen flow started.
HOW TO KNOW WHEN THE OXYGEN FLOW STOPS
The crew must be aware
of the indications when the oxygen flow stops. When the oxygen flow
stops, the crew must remove the  PBE .
Refer to the documentation of the manufacturer for the indications
when the oxygen supply stops.
Each  PBE  model may
have different indications when the oxygen supply stops.
When the oxygen supply stops or if the oxygen supply is not able
to be activated or if the  PBE  malfunctions, the user must
immediately remove the  PBE .
PBE  REMOVAL
Do not smoke or go
near fire after the removal of the  PBE , because there may
be a lot of oxygen on the hair.
The  PBE  may still generate oxygen for a period of time
after it is removed.
Therefore, the  PBE  must be removed away from areas with smoke/fire.  After the activation
of the  PBE , the generator may be hot after use. Therefore
the user should not touch the generator.
Do not touch the  PBE  generator after it is activated.
Put the  PBE  on a heat resistant surface, to enable the generator to cool down.
For more information refer to the documentation
of the manufacturer.
GPS Interference
- Within the Interference Area - General
WITHIN THE INTERFERENCE AREA
A/C POS  MONITOR
The flight crew must
regularly monitor the aircraft position using non-GPS references.
GPS DESELECTION  CONSIDER
At any time, in the
case of expected spoofing or detected  FMS  position shift
(  to access the list
of effects), the flight crew should consider  GPS  deselection
on the  FMS  page SELECTED NAVAIDS.
FMS  navigation modes revert to  IRS / DME / DME ,  IRS / VOR / DME  or  IRS  only
The  GPS  deselection only affect the  FMS  position computation.
Other aircraft systems will continue to use the  GPS  data
if available (aircraft clock,  TAWS ,  ADS-B  out,
etc.)
The  GPS  deselection on one  MCDU  side applies to both  FMS .
If  FMS  position shift detected:
Use  AP / FD  on reliable  FMS  side
If both  FMS  position erroneous:
HDG/TRK MODE  SELECT
If expected undue predictive TAWS alerts:
GPWS TERR  OFF  CONSIDER
The basic  GPWS  modes remain operative. For more information about the consequences
of the predictive modes inhibition,  .
In cruise above  MSA , the flight crew can set  GPWS TERR  to OFF.  In other flight phases,
the Operator must perform a safety assessment based on their knowledge
of operations to adapt the procedures and pilot briefings to specific
routes.
ATC  NOTIFY
The flight crew should notify
the  ATC  of any suspected interference during the flight
(with the observed effects on the aircraft systems).
